storm.summary_layperson: No storm threat for the cove this evening — radar is clear and the atmosphere has essentially no fuel for thunderstorms (CAPE near zero) as temperatures cool after sunset.
storm.local_effect_blurb: The Sound (73°F) is running warmer than the air (66°F and falling toward 63°F by 8 PM), so there's no protective marine layer tonight — but with no storms anywhere near the area, that doesn't matter for this window.
storm.detail_html:
No thunderstorm risk is on the table for the 5–10 PM window. HRRR keeps CAPE at essentially zero (0–30 J/kg) through the period, and the latest OKX forecast discussion has SBCAPE below 100 J/kg with plenty of CIN (a capping layer) holding any lift down. Radar out of KOKX shows no echoes anywhere near the approach sectors, and there are no active NWS watches, warnings, or advisories.

Deep-layer shear is actually strong (48–60 kt out of the west), but shear without instability doesn't organize anything — it's a non-factor tonight.

The marine layer isn't a factor either, in either direction. The Sound is running warmer than the air, which is the opposite setup from the stable, storm-choking marine layer the cove sometimes gets on hot summer afternoons. That protective mechanism needs cold water under warm air; tonight it's inverted, so there's no buffer — but since nothing is approaching, it doesn't matter.

Bottom line for the cove and surrounding towns alike: a quiet, mostly clear evening with no meaningful storm risk anywhere in the wider Sound.

wind.tactics_blurb: Light, wandering gradient breeze (4–8 kt) with no sea breeze to lean on — stay center and play shifts as they come rather than committing to a side.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
This is a light gradient-wind evening, not a sea-breeze day. The thermal gate never engaged — Long Island Sound water (73°F) is actually warmer than the air (66°F), so there's no land-sea contrast to drive a classic afternoon sea breeze, and only 25% of coastal stations are reading southerly versus the roughly 50%+ needed to call a mature thermal in place.

HRRR has the window running light and ENE (4–6 kt) through 6–7 PM, veering to SE and freshening to around 8 kt by 8 PM. That's a real divergence worth flagging: Riverside YC's own station is already reading SE at 5.3 kt with gusts to 7 right now, 65° off the model's ENE call. The model looks to be behind the actual wind — expect the SE veer it shows for 8 PM to arrive earlier than forecast.

HRRR's forecast hours only extend to 8:00 PM this run (the later forecast hours failed to fetch), so 9 and 10 PM aren't covered by model data — treat the back half of the window as an extrapolation from the 8 PM trend (SE, freshening slightly) rather than a hard forecast.

With no dominant thermal engine and the wind still finding its direction, there's no strong case for either side of the course. Favor the center and play shifts as they come — a fleet leaning hard on one side in a wandering 4–8 kt gradient breeze is more likely to get burned by a shift than rewarded for a read.
